questions.question_text: A particle has position $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(-4+3t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(6-2t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres, where $t$ is in seconds. What is its position vector when $t=5$?

options.why: Treated the $-2t$ term as $+2t$, giving $6+10=16$ for the second component.
Added the velocity once instead of five times, that is, substituted $t=1$.
Substituted $t=1$ and also treated the $-2t$ term as $+2t$.

questions.question_text: A helicopter is at the point with position vector $\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ km when $t=0$, and flies with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix}-3\\5\end{pmatrix}$ km/h. Which expression gives its position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$?

options.why: Swapped the roles of the two vectors, multiplying the initial position by $t$ instead of the velocity.
Subtracted the velocity instead of adding it, reversing the direction of travel.
Swapped the roles of the two vectors and also reversed the direction of travel.

questions.question_text: A particle moves with constant velocity. At $t=3$ s it is at the point $(7,-2)$ and at $t=8$ s it is at the point $(-3,13)$, with distances in metres. What is its velocity vector?

options.why: Found the displacement but forgot to divide by the $5$ seconds taken.
Subtracted the positions the wrong way round, giving the velocity reversed.
Subtracted the positions the wrong way round and did not divide by the $5$ seconds.

questions.question_text: A particle has position $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(-2+5t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(4-12t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres, where $t$ is in seconds. How fast is the particle moving?

options.why: Added the sizes of the velocity components, $5+12$, instead of using Pythagoras.
Combined the components before squaring, computing $\sqrt{(5-12)^{2}}$ because the $\underset{\sim}{j}$ component is negative, instead of squaring each component first.
Added the sizes of the components of the initial position vector, $2+4$, instead of using the velocity.

questions.question_text: A particle has position $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(-9+4t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(20-6t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres, where $t$ is in seconds. At what time is the particle at the point $(7,-4)$?

options.why: Solved $4t=7$, ignoring the initial position $-9$ in the first component.
Moved the $-9$ to the other side with the wrong sign, solving $4t=7-9$ as $4t=-16$.
Ignored the initial position and also used the wrong sign, solving $4t=-7$.

questions.solution_text:
$-9+4t=7$
$4t=16$
$t=4$
Checking the $\underset{\sim}{j}$ component:
$20-6\times 4$
$=-4$
The particle is at $(7,-4)$ when $t=4$ s.

questions.question_text: Two ships have positions $\underset{\sim}{r}_{A}(t)=(3+2t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(-5+6t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{r}_{B}(t)=(11-4t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(7-2t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ kilometres, where $t$ is in hours. What is the exact distance between the ships when $t=2$?

options.why: Added the two component differences, $4+4$, instead of using Pythagoras.
Added the two position vectors instead of subtracting them before using Pythagoras.
Added the two position vectors and then added the components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.question_text: Particle $P$ has position $\underset{\sim}{r}_{P}(t)=(1+3t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2+t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ and particle $Q$ has position $\underset{\sim}{r}_{Q}(t)=(16-2t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(-4+5t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres, where $t$ is in seconds. Do the particles collide?

options.text: No, because the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ components are equal at $t=3$ but the $\underset{\sim}{j}$ components are equal at $t=1.5$.
No, because the paths of the two particles never cross.
options.why: Assumes that no collision means the paths do not meet, but these paths do cross; the particles simply pass that point at different times.
Solved only the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ components and did not check that the $\underset{\sim}{j}$ components agree at the same time.
Solved only the $\underset{\sim}{j}$ components and did not check that the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ components agree at the same time.

questions.solution_text:
Equating the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ components:
$1+3t=16-2t$
$5t=15$
$t=3$
Equating the $\underset{\sim}{j}$ components:
$2+t=-4+5t$
$4t=6$
$t=1.5$
The two times are different, so the particles are never at the same point at the same time.
The particles do not collide.

questions.question_text: A particle $A$ has position $\underset{\sim}{r}_{A}(t)=(-2+3t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(5+2t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres, where $t$ is in seconds. A particle $B$ starts at the point $(43,55)$ at $t=0$ and travels with constant velocity so that it collides with $A$ when $t=5$. What is the velocity of $B$, and how fast is $B$ moving?

options.why: Subtracted the positions the wrong way round, so the velocity points away from the collision point.
Used the displacement as the velocity, forgetting to divide by the $5$ seconds.
Subtracted the positions the wrong way round and also forgot to divide by the $5$ seconds.
